Luxembourg 96%. Belgium 86%. France over 90%. Cross one more border and it falls to 14%, then 4%, then 1%. French in Europe has a core and a long tail, and almost nothing in between.

a thread 🧵🗺️

1/ The figures come from Eurobarometer 386, the EU's 2012 language survey. They are self-reported — people saying they could hold a conversation, not sitting an exam. Read every number as confidence as much as ability.

2/ Luxembourg's 96% is the strangest on the map. Only about 16% called French their first language. Nearly the whole country acquired it. French is still the language Luxembourg writes its laws in, a leftover of the Napoleonic Code.
3/ It had native French speakers once. The partition of 1839 handed its Walloon districts to Belgium, leaving a state whose everyday speech is Germanic and whose statute book is Romance.

4/ Belgium's 86% runs the other way. French is one of three official languages, but Dutch-speaking Flanders is the larger half. The number is high because a bilingual country sits inside it — not because Belgium is French.
5/ Then the cliff. Germany 14%, Austria 11%, Poland 4%, Hungary 3%, Slovakia 2%, Czechia 1%. French thins out almost exactly where it stops being the language of the paperwork next door.

6/ Romania at 17% breaks the pattern — as high as Britain, with no French border and no French colonial past. French was the language of its 19th-century elite, it joined the Francophonie in 1993, and the schools never quite let go.
7/ Note who is missing. Switzerland is blank, and French is one of its official languages. Eurobarometer only surveyed EU members, so the map's black isn't ignorance — it's a sampling frame.

8/ One thing the map can't show: across the EU, French is still the most widely spoken foreign language after English. It just isn't anyone's second language in particular — a thin layer spread very wide.

Follow @forummapping for more maps like this.
